absorption-coefficient.short: How quickly light of a given wavelength is absorbed as it travels into a material, per unit length. Its inverse is the absorption depth: the distance at which about 63 % of the light has been absorbed.

actuator-disc.short: An idealised rotor treated as a thin, permeable disc that takes energy from the flow. The simplest model that gives the Betz limit.

aerodynamic-lift.short: The force on a wing or blade at right angles to the air flowing past it. On a wind turbine blade the lift points mostly downwind, but it leans slightly forward along the rotation, and that small forward part turns the rotor.

aerodynamic-stall.short: When the angle of attack gets too large, air peels away from the top of the blade: lift collapses and drag soars.

air-mass.short: How many atmospheres' worth of air sunlight crosses to reach you: 1 with the Sun overhead, about 1.5 at 48° from overhead, and more as the Sun sinks.

albedo.short: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects, from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything). Fresh snow and white gravel reflect far more than grass or dark soil.

amorphous-silicon.short: Silicon with no long-range crystal order, deposited from a gas as a very thin film. Absorbs light strongly but converts it less efficiently than crystal silicon.

anaerobic-digestion.short: Microbes breaking down wet organic matter (manure, food waste, sewage) without oxygen, producing biogas that is mostly methane and carbon dioxide.

angle-of-attack.short: The angle between a blade's chord line and the air flowing past it. A few degrees gives strong lift; too many and the flow separates and the blade stalls.

angle-of-incidence.short: The angle between incoming sunlight and a line sticking straight out of a panel. At 0° the panel faces the Sun square on and catches the most light.

anti-islanding.short: A required inverter safety function: if the grid goes down, the inverter stops feeding power so it cannot energise lines that line workers believe are dead.

anti-reflection-coating.short: A very thin transparent layer on top of a cell, about a quarter of a wavelength of light thick, that cancels reflections so more light goes in. It gives silicon cells their dark blue look.

apparent-wind.short: The wind a moving blade actually feels: the real wind combined with the headwind from the blade's own motion. Near the tips it is mostly the blade's own speed.

back-contact-cell.short: A cell with all of its metal contacts on the back, in interleaved fingers, so nothing shades the front. Holds the silicon efficiency records.

balance-of-system.short: Everything in a solar installation except the modules: mounting structures, trackers, cables, connectors, fuses, switches, inverters and monitoring.

band-gap.short: The minimum energy an electron in a semiconductor must gain to break free and carry current. Silicon's is about 1.12 eV.

beccs.term: BECCS (bioenergy with carbon capture and storage)
beccs.short: Burning or fermenting biomass for energy, then capturing the carbon dioxide and storing it underground, so that the carbon the plants took from the air stays out of it.

betz-limit.short: No wind turbine can capture more than 16/27, about 59 %, of the power in the wind passing through its rotor.

bifacial-module.short: A solar panel that collects light on both faces: sunlight on the front plus light reflected from the ground onto the back.

binary-cycle-plant.short: A geothermal plant in which hot brine heats a second fluid with a low boiling point; that fluid's vapour drives the turbine. Works with cooler resources.

biofuel.short: A liquid or gaseous fuel made from biomass, such as ethanol from sugarcane or corn, or biodiesel from vegetable oils.

biomass.short: Plant and animal material (wood, crop waste, manure, energy crops) used as fuel. Its energy came from sunlight captured by photosynthesis.

blackbody.short: An idealised object that absorbs all light and glows with a spectrum set only by its temperature. The Sun's light is close to that of a blackbody at about 5772 K.

blade-pitch.short: Twisting a whole blade about its long axis. Turbines pitch their blades to catch the most power in light winds and to shed power in strong winds.

built-in-potential.short: The voltage step across a p-n junction in the dark, created by the fixed charges in the depletion region. About 0.6 to 0.9 V in silicon.

bypass-diode.short: A one-way electrical valve wired across a group of cells. If a cell in the group is shaded, the string's current flows around the group through the diode instead of being blocked.

cadmium-telluride.short: A compound semiconductor with a band gap near 1.5 eV, deposited as a thin film on glass. The leading thin-film technology, made mainly by First Solar.

capacity-factor.short: Energy a plant actually produces in a year divided by what it would produce running flat out all year.

capital-recovery-factor.short: The share of an up-front cost that must be paid each year, like a mortgage payment, to repay it with interest over its lifetime.

carbon-debt.short: The extra carbon dioxide released when land is cleared to grow bioenergy crops. It takes years of replacing fossil fuel before the savings repay it.

carnot-efficiency.short: The highest share of heat any engine could turn into work between a hot and a cold temperature: 1 minus cold over hot, in kelvin.

certified-efficiency.short: An efficiency measured by an independent, accredited test lab (such as NREL, Fraunhofer ISE CalLab, ISFH or ESTI) under standard test conditions, rather than by the team that made the cell.

cigs.short: A thin-film semiconductor whose band gap can be tuned by swapping gallium for indium. Can be made on flexible foils.

clear-sky-model.short: A formula for how much sunlight reaches the ground on a cloudless day. It gives a ceiling: real days with clouds and haze bring less.

clipping.short: When the panels could deliver more power than the inverter's rating, the inverter caps its output and the extra is not collected. Shows up as a flat top on a sunny day's power curve.

co2-equivalent.short: A way to add different greenhouse gases together: each gas is counted as the mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the planet as much over 100 years.

concentrated-solar-power.short: Mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid; the heat drives a turbine like a conventional power station. Also called solar thermal electricity.

concentration-ratio.short: How many times a concentrator multiplies sunlight: the mirror aperture area divided by the receiver area. Troughs reach roughly tens to about a hundred; towers hundreds to about a thousand.

concentrator-photovoltaics.short: Solar cells placed under lenses or mirrors that focus sunlight many times over, so a tiny, expensive cell does the work of a large one.

conduction-band.short: The range of energies at which an electron is free to wander through the crystal and carry current. It sits one band gap above the valence band.

conversion-efficiency.short: The share of the sunlight power landing on a cell that comes out as electrical power, measured at standard test conditions.

cost-of-capital.short: The yearly return lenders and investors demand for financing a plant, usually a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of debt and equity. It is the discount rate in an LCOE.

cumulative-capacity.short: All the generating capacity ever installed and still counted, added up. For learning curves, the total ever produced is what matters.

current-matching.short: In a stack wired in series, the same current must flow through every cell, so the cell that makes the least current sets it. Designers choose band gaps so each cell makes about the same current.

curtailment.short: Turning down wind or solar output that could have been generated, because the grid cannot use or store it at that moment.

cut-in-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine starts producing power, typically about 3 m/s.

cut-out-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine stops to protect itself, typically 25 m/s or more.

czochralski-process.short: A way to grow one large, nearly flawless crystal: dip a small seed crystal into molten material and pull it up slowly while turning it. Most single-crystal silicon is made this way.

dc-ac-ratio.short: Panel power (DC, at standard test conditions) divided by inverter power (AC). Above 1, the panels can sometimes make more than the inverter can pass.

degradation-rate.short: How fast a panel's output falls with age, in % per year. Field studies find about half a percent per year is typical.

demand-response.short: Moving or trimming electricity use when the grid is stretched: heating water at noon instead of evening, pausing car charging, industry cutting load for a fee.

depletion-region.short: The thin layer around a p-n junction that has been emptied of free carriers, leaving fixed charged atoms that set up an electric field.

detailed-balance.short: The principle that, in equilibrium, every process runs as often as its reverse. For a solar cell: a material that absorbs light well must also emit light, so some energy always leaks back out.

diffuse-horizontal-irradiance.short: Sunlight scattered by air, haze and clouds that arrives from the rest of the sky, measured on a flat horizontal surface, in W/m².

diffusion.short: Carriers spreading from where they are crowded to where they are scarce, just by random motion.

direct-band-gap.short: A band gap where an electron can jump from the top of the valence band to the bottom of the conduction band by absorbing a photon alone. Such materials (GaAs, CdTe, perovskites) absorb sunlight in a layer a few microns thick.

direct-normal-irradiance.short: Sunlight coming straight from the Sun's disc, measured on a surface turned to face the Sun square on, in W/m².

discount-rate.short: How much less money in the future is worth than money today, in percent per year. It stands for interest and the return investors expect.

dispatch.short: Deciding, minute by minute, which power plants and stores run and how hard, so that supply matches demand.

dispatchable.short: A source that can raise or lower its output when the grid operator asks, such as hydro with a reservoir, geothermal, bioenergy or gas. Sun and wind are not, unless paired with storage.

district-heating.short: Heating many buildings from one central source through a network of insulated hot-water pipes.

doping.short: Adding a tiny, controlled amount of another element to a pure semiconductor to give it spare electrons (n-type) or spare holes (p-type).

drift.short: Carriers moving because an electric field pushes them: electrons against the field, holes along it.

dry-steam-plant.short: A geothermal plant fed directly by natural steam from the ground, the oldest kind (Larderello, The Geysers).

duck-curve.short: The shape of net load on a sunny spring day in a grid with lots of solar: a deep midday belly and a steep evening climb as the Sun sets. Named by the California grid operator.

ebb-generation.short: Running a tidal barrage's turbines as the basin empties towards a falling sea, after trapping water at high tide.

electrolysis.short: Using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can be stored and later turned back into electricity or used as a fuel.

electron-hole-pair.short: A free electron and the hole it left behind, created together when a photon with enough energy is absorbed.

electronvolt.short: The energy one electron gains crossing one volt: 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules. Handy for photons: visible light carries 1.6 to 3.3 eV.

emitter.short: The thin, heavily doped layer on one side of a solar cell that forms the p-n junction with the bulk wafer and collects one type of carrier.

energy-period.short: The wave period that, in a sea of mixed waves, gives the same energy flux as a regular wave with that period. Used with significant wave height to size wave power.

energy-storage.short: Holding energy now to deliver it later: batteries, pumped hydro, hydrogen, heat. Rated by power (MW, how fast) and energy (MWh, how much).

enhanced-geothermal-system.short: Man-made geothermal: fluid is pumped into hot, dry rock to open fractures, so water can be circulated through the rock and heated.

equation-of-time.short: How far a sundial runs ahead of or behind an even clock, up to about 16 minutes, because Earth's orbit is an ellipse and its axis is tilted.

feed-in-tariff.short: A law that guarantees a fixed price, for many years, for each kilowatt-hour a renewable generator feeds into the grid. It makes small and large projects easy to finance.

fill-factor.short: The maximum power divided by Voc × Isc. It says how square the I-V curve is; good silicon cells reach about 0.8 or more.

flash-steam-plant.short: A geothermal plant that drops the pressure of very hot water from the well so part of it boils (flashes) into steam, which drives a turbine. Needs fluid above about 182 °C.

flow-battery.short: A battery whose energy is stored in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks and pumped through a cell stack. Bigger tanks mean more hours of storage.

francis-turbine.short: A reaction turbine in which water spirals inward through a spinning runner whose curved blades are fixed in shape (not adjustable). The workhorse of medium- to high-head hydropower.

frequency.short: How many wave crests pass a point each second, written f and measured in hertz (Hz). For light, f = c/λ, so shorter wavelengths mean higher frequencies.

fuel-cell.short: A device that combines hydrogen with oxygen to make electricity, water and heat directly, without burning.

full-load-hours.short: A year's output expressed as hours at nameplate capacity: capacity factor × 8,760. A solar farm with a capacity factor of 0.17 makes as much as 1,489 hours at full power.

gasification.short: Heating biomass with too little oxygen to burn it fully, turning it into a combustible gas of carbon monoxide and hydrogen (syngas).

global-horizontal-irradiance.short: All the sunlight reaching flat, level ground: the direct beam times the cosine of the zenith angle, plus the diffuse light. Weather stations usually measure this.

grid-forming-inverter.short: An inverter that sets its own voltage and frequency, like a spinning generator does, instead of following the grid's. It can help steady a grid with little spinning inertia.

grid-frequency.short: How many times per second alternating current reverses: 50 Hz in most of the world, 60 Hz in North America, parts of South America and parts of Asia. It dips when demand exceeds supply and rises when supply exceeds demand.

half-cut-cells.short: Full-size cells cut in two with a laser. Each half carries half the current, so the wiring wastes less power as heat.

heliostat.short: A flat, steerable mirror that tracks the Sun so that it always reflects sunlight onto the same fixed target, such as the receiver on top of a tower.

heterojunction-cell.short: A silicon cell sandwiched between very thin layers of amorphous silicon, which passivate the surfaces and form the junction. High voltage and a small temperature loss.

hole.short: The gap left where an electron is missing from a bond. It moves through the crystal like a positive charge.

hot-carrier-cell.short: A proposed solar cell that collects electrons before they cool down, keeping the energy that ordinary cells lose as heat.

hot-spot.short: A shaded or damaged cell that the rest of the string forces into reverse bias, so that it absorbs power instead of making it and turns it into heat. It can burn the module unless a bypass diode steps in.

hvdc.short: Transmission by direct current at hundreds of kilovolts or more. Loses less energy than alternating current over long distances and under the sea, and links grids that are not synchronised.

hydraulic-head.short: The height that water falls between the intake and the turbine of a hydropower plant, in metres.

ideality-factor.short: A number, usually between 1 and 2, that says how closely a diode follows the ideal diode law. Higher values mean more recombination in the junction and a rounder I-V curve.

indirect-band-gap.short: A band gap where the jump also needs a kick of momentum from a lattice vibration (phonon). Absorption near the gap is weak, which is why silicon cells are made from wafers far thicker than thin-film cells.

induction-factor.short: How much a rotor slows the wind as it passes through, as a fraction of the free wind speed. The ideal rotor slows it by one third.

inertia.short: The energy stored in the spinning turbines and generators of a grid. It resists sudden changes in frequency, buying a few seconds for reserves to respond.

ingot.short: A large solid block of crystal, grown or cast from molten material, that is later sliced into wafers.

insolation.short: Sunlight energy collected over a period, usually in kWh/m² per day or per year. Daily insolation in kWh/m² equals peak sun hours.

installed-cost.short: Everything it takes to build a power plant and connect it, divided by its nameplate capacity, in US dollars per kilowatt (US$/kW).

interconnector.short: A transmission line or cable linking two grids, often between countries, so each can import when short and export when in surplus.

intermediate-band-cell.short: A proposed solar cell with an extra energy level inside the band gap, so two low-energy photons can together lift one electron across.

intrinsic-carrier-density.short: How many free electrons (and equally many holes) pure, undoped silicon has from heat alone: about 10¹⁰ per cubic centimetre at room temperature.

inverter.short: The box that turns the panels' direct current (DC) into alternating current (AC) in step with the grid, and keeps the panels at their best operating point.

irradiance.short: Sunlight power arriving per square metre, in watts per square metre (W/m²). Bright midday sun is about 1000 W/m².

isotropic-sky-model.short: The simplifying assumption that diffuse sky light is equally bright from every part of the sky, so a tilted panel collects it in proportion to how much sky it can see.

iv-curve.short: A graph of the current a solar cell delivers against its voltage, from short circuit to open circuit.

kaplan-turbine.short: A propeller-shaped reaction turbine with adjustable blades, suited to low heads and large flows.

land-use-intensity.short: Land occupied per unit of electricity produced each year, for example square metres per MWh/yr. It can count only the direct footprint or the whole site and the mines that feed it.

lcoe.short: The average price per unit of energy a plant must earn over its life to pay back its building, running and financing costs.

learning-rate.short: The share by which a technology's cost falls each time the total amount ever produced doubles.

lifecycle-emissions.short: All the greenhouse gases released to make, run and dispose of an energy source, counted per unit of energy it delivers: farming, fertiliser, transport, processing and land-use change included.

linear-fresnel.short: Rows of long, nearly flat mirror strips that each tilt to send sunlight onto a fixed pipe above them: a cheaper, flatter cousin of the parabolic trough.

lithium-ion.short: A rechargeable battery in which lithium ions shuttle between two electrodes. Grid batteries mostly use the LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry; many cars use NMC (nickel manganese cobalt).

maximum-power-point.short: The point on the I-V curve where current × voltage is largest. Inverters keep panels there by tracking it (MPPT).

module-efficiency.short: The share of sunlight falling on a whole solar panel, frame and gaps included, that comes out as electricity. Lower than cell efficiency because of the gaps, wiring and edges.

molten-salt.short: A mix of sodium and potassium nitrates, liquid from roughly 240 °C up to about 565 °C, used to carry and store heat in CSP plants.

monocrystalline-silicon.short: Silicon in which the whole wafer is one continuous crystal, with every atom lined up. Grown with the Czochralski process.

mppt.short: The inverter's job of constantly adjusting the panels' operating voltage to sit at the maximum power point as sun and temperature change.

multicrystalline-silicon.short: Silicon cast as a block that freezes into many crystal grains. Cheaper to make, but the boundaries between grains trap charge carriers.

multijunction-cell.short: A solar cell built from several stacked cells with different band gaps, each converting its own slice of the spectrum. A two-junction cell is a tandem.

n-type.short: Silicon doped with an element such as phosphorus, whose atoms each give up one extra electron. Electrons are the majority carriers.

nameplate-capacity.short: The most power a plant is built to deliver, in kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW). A 100 MW solar farm makes 100 MW only in full sun.

net-load.short: Demand minus the output of wind and solar: what the rest of the grid (hydro, gas, storage, imports) must supply.

noct.short: The temperature a module's cells reach in a standard outdoor-like test: 800 W/m², 20 °C air, a 1 m/s breeze. Usually 40–45 °C.

open-circuit-voltage.short: The voltage across a cell when nothing is connected and no current flows. About 0.6 to 0.75 V for silicon cells.

operations-and-maintenance.short: The yearly cost of running a plant: staff, repairs, insurance, land lease. Fixed O&M is per kW per year; variable O&M is per MWh produced.

oscillating-water-column.short: A wave device with an air chamber open to the sea below: waves push the trapped air back and forth through a turbine.

p-type.short: Silicon doped with an element such as boron, whose atoms each accept an electron and leave a hole behind. Holes are the majority carriers.

parabolic-trough.short: A long, curved mirror that focuses sunlight onto a pipe running along its focal line. The whole trough turns to follow the Sun.

partial-shading.short: When part of an array is shaded (by a chimney, a tree, leaves or dirt) and the rest is not. Because cells are in series, a little shade can cost a lot of power.

passivation.short: Treating a surface so it stops swallowing electrons and holes. Bare crystal surfaces have broken bonds where carriers recombine; a thin coating ties them up.

peak-sun-hours.short: A day's sunlight energy expressed as hours of 1000 W/m² sunshine. 5 kWh/m² in a day is 5 peak sun hours.

pelton-turbine.short: An impulse turbine: jets of water hit a ring of split cups. Suited to very high heads and small flows.

penstock.short: The large pipe that carries water from a reservoir's intake down to the turbines.

perc.short: A silicon cell whose back surface is coated with a passivating layer, with only small laser-cut openings for the metal contact. The industry's workhorse until TOPCon overtook it in 2024.

performance-ratio.short: The share of a solar array's ideal output that actually reaches the grid after losses to heat, wiring, the inverter, dirt and shading. Typically 0.75 to 0.85.

perovskite.short: A family of crystals with the same arrangement of atoms as the mineral perovskite. Metal-halide perovskites absorb sunlight strongly and can be made from solution at low temperature.

perturb-and-observe.short: The simplest MPPT method: nudge the voltage, check whether power went up, and keep going that way if it did, or turn back if it did not.

phonon.short: A packet of vibration of the crystal lattice: a quantum of heat and sound in a solid. Electrons shed excess energy by emitting phonons.

photoconductivity.short: A material conducts electricity better when light shines on it, because light frees extra charge carriers. It needs an outside battery; it does not make power by itself.

photoelectric-effect.short: Light knocks electrons out of a metal surface. Einstein explained it in 1905 by treating light as packets (photons), each with energy set by its colour.

photon.short: A single packet of light. Its energy is set by its colour: bluer light comes in bigger packets.

photosynthesis.short: How plants, algae and some bacteria use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen. The sugars store the sunlight's energy as chemical energy.

photovoltaic-effect.short: Light falling on a material produces a voltage and can drive a current, with no moving parts. It is how every solar cell works.

plane-of-array-irradiance.short: The sunlight landing on the face of a tilted panel, in W/m²: the direct beam plus the share of sky light and ground reflection the panel can see.

pn-junction.short: The boundary inside one crystal where p-type silicon meets n-type silicon. Its built-in electric field separates light-made electrons and holes.

polysilicon.short: Ultra-pure silicon made of many small crystals; the raw material melted down to grow the crystals that are sliced into solar wafers.

power-coefficient.short: The share of the wind's power flowing through a rotor that the turbine captures. It can never exceed the Betz limit.

power-tower.short: A CSP plant in which a field of heliostats reflects sunlight onto a receiver at the top of a central tower. Also called a central receiver.

pumped-storage.short: Two reservoirs at different heights: pump water uphill when power is cheap and plentiful, let it run back down through turbines when it is needed. By energy stored, the largest form of grid storage.

rated-wind-speed.short: The wind speed at which a turbine first reaches its full (rated) power. Above it the blades pitch to hold power steady.

rayleigh-distribution.short: A simple bell-with-a-long-tail curve for how often each wind speed occurs at a site, set by one number: the mean wind speed.

recombination.short: A free electron falling back into a hole. The pair's energy is lost as heat or light and can no longer drive a current.

reinjection-well.short: A well that returns cooled geothermal water to the reservoir, keeping up pressure and disposing of the brine.

research-cell.short: A small, hand-made laboratory solar cell, often under 1 cm², built to show how far a technology can go. Its record efficiency is higher than any module you can buy.

rocof.short: How fast grid frequency moves after a sudden loss of supply or demand, in hertz per second. Less inertia means a faster change.

round-trip-efficiency.short: The share of energy you get back from a store after putting it in: the efficiencies of charging and discharging multiplied together.

run-of-river.short: A plant that uses a river's flow as it comes, with little or no reservoir, so its output follows the river.

saturation-current.short: The tiny leakage current of a diode in the dark, set by recombination. The smaller it is, the higher the cell's voltage.

semiconductor.short: A material, such as silicon, that conducts electricity much better than an insulator but much worse than a metal, and whose conductivity can be tuned.

sensible-heat.short: Heat stored by raising a material's temperature (as opposed to melting it). Stored energy = mass × specific heat × temperature rise.

series-resistance.short: Resistance in the path current must travel: the silicon itself, the metal fingers and the contacts. It tilts the right side of the I-V curve.

shockley-queisser-limit.short: The highest efficiency a single-junction solar cell can reach in ordinary sunlight, about 33 % at a band gap near 1.34 eV.

short-circuit-current.short: The current a cell delivers when its terminals are wired straight together, so the voltage is zero. It grows in proportion to the light.

shunt-resistance.short: A leakage path that lets current sneak around the junction instead of going to the load. Low values tilt the flat top of the I-V curve.

significant-wave-height.short: The average height of the tallest third of the waves, about what an observer would judge by eye. Used to size wave energy.

smart-grid.short: A grid with sensors, communications and automatic controls, so that generation, storage and demand can be monitored and coordinated in near real time.

solar-azimuth.short: The compass direction of the Sun, in degrees clockwise from north: 90° east, 180° south, 270° west.

solar-declination.short: The latitude where the Sun is directly overhead at noon. Because Earth's axis is tilted, it swings between about +23.4° in June and −23.4° in December, passing 0° at the equinoxes.

solar-dish.short: A dish-shaped mirror that focuses sunlight onto a point receiver, often driving a small Stirling engine. Reaches the highest concentrations but is built in small units.

solar-elevation.short: How high the Sun stands above the horizon, in degrees: 0° at sunrise and sunset, 90° straight overhead.

solar-module.short: What most people call a solar panel: many cells wired together, laminated between glass and a back sheet, with a frame and a junction box.

solar-time.short: Time set by the Sun rather than by time zones: the Sun crosses due north or south at about 12:00 solar time. Clocks can differ from it by an hour or more.

solar-tracker.short: A motorised mount that turns panels to follow the Sun across the sky, usually rotating east to west about one axis.

solar-zenith-angle.short: The angle between the Sun and the point straight overhead. It is 90° minus the solar elevation.

standard-test-conditions.short: The agreed lab conditions for rating solar cells: 1000 W/m² of light with the AM1.5 spectrum and a cell temperature of 25 °C.

state-of-charge.short: How full a store is, as energy (MWh) or as a percentage of its capacity.

storage-duration.short: How many hours a store can deliver at its full power: energy capacity (MWh) divided by power rating (MW). A 100 MW / 400 MWh battery is a 4-hour battery.

string.short: Solar modules wired one after another in series, so their voltages add. Several strings in parallel make an array.

swansons-law.short: The solar version of Wright's law: module prices fall by a steady share each time the total ever shipped doubles. Named after Richard Swanson, founder of the solar company SunPower.

tailrace.short: The channel that carries water away from a turbine back to the river.

tandem-cell.short: A solar cell made of two or more stacked cells with different band gaps, so each band of colours is caught by the gap that wastes least of it.

temperature-coefficient.short: How much a panel's power (or voltage) changes for each degree of warming, in % per °C. Silicon panels lose roughly 0.3 % of power per °C above 25 °C.

thermalisation.short: The fast loss, as heat, of whatever energy a photon had above the band gap. The freed electron (and hole) shake the crystal lattice and settle to the band edge within about a trillionth of a second.

thin-film.short: A cell made by depositing a semiconductor layer a few micrometres thick onto glass, metal or plastic, instead of slicing a wafer.

tidal-barrage.short: A dam across an estuary or bay with sluices and turbines. It traps the tide and generates as water runs through the turbines across the height difference.

tidal-range.short: The height difference between high and low water. Barrages need large ranges, several metres or more.

tidal-stream.short: An underwater turbine placed in a fast tidal current, working like a wind turbine in water.

tip-speed-ratio.short: How fast the blade tips move compared with the wind. Large modern rotors run with their tips several times faster than the wind.

topcon.short: A silicon cell whose back contact sits on an ultra-thin oxide plus a doped polysilicon layer, so carriers can pass but the surface stays passivated. The most-made cell type today.

transparent-conductive-oxide.short: A coating, such as indium tin oxide or doped zinc oxide, that conducts electricity yet lets light through. Used on heterojunction and thin-film cells.

typical-meteorological-year.short: A year of hourly weather stitched together from real months that are typical for a site, used to estimate long-run solar output.

valence-band.short: The range of energies held by electrons that are tied up in the bonds between atoms. Electrons there cannot carry current on their own.

variable-renewable.short: Sources whose output follows the weather and time of day rather than demand, chiefly wind and solar photovoltaics.

wafer.short: A thin slice of crystal cut from an ingot with a wire saw. Solar wafers are about 0.14 mm thick, roughly two human hairs.

wave-energy-flux.short: Power carried by waves across each metre of wave crest, in kilowatts per metre. Exposed Atlantic coasts often average several tens of kW/m.

wavelength.short: The distance from one crest of a light wave to the next, written λ (lambda) and measured here in nanometres (nm). Visible light spans about 380 to 750 nm.

wrights-law.short: The observation that cost falls by a steady percentage every time cumulative production doubles.
